[Addiction, Faith, and the Limits of Willpower](https://www.econtalk.org/addiction-faith-and-the-limits-of-willpower-with-meghan-ogieblyn/),
EconTalk, 5 October 2026
([Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/1sRLtmRNeZ3DWmXgnGLcJQ)).

> We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will.
>
> --- Simone Weil

Meghan O'Gieblyn takes the line from Weil as the starting point of her memoir
*Will and Attention*, which she discusses with Russ Roberts. The book follows
her drinking, her recovery and her loss of faith, and draws on Weil, William
James and Iris Murdoch, who argue that the will is powerless over the things a
person most wants to change.

- **Attention as directed receptivity.** O'Gieblyn describes attention as
  observing without grasping, rather than as rigid focus.
- **The choices in between the choices.** The choices that shape a life most are
  the ones a person barely notices making.
- **Reasoning toward harm.** A person can reason their way into doing something
  destructive, which is one reason effort alone does not stop it.

## Five Ways to Grow Up

Roberts says that "part of growing up is becoming self-aware and realizing
you're not the center of the universe, which is the way human beings start."
He names "four ways to grow up and become self-aware: religion, meditation,
literature, therapy." O'Gieblyn adds a fifth, suffering, which is the hard way.
The other four are a way to learn without it:

> The ideal of any kind of religious pursuit or moral pursuit is to try to
> change and improve without having to constantly suffer consequences before
> you do.
>
> --- Meghan O'Gieblyn

## Schopenhauer on the Will

O'Gieblyn quotes Schopenhauer: a person can act on what they want, but cannot
choose what to want. The desire comes from somewhere the will does not reach.

> Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills.
>
> --- Arthur Schopenhauer, *On the Freedom of the Will*

## William James on Change

Both lines are from the episode, drawing on William James's *The Varieties of
Religious Experience*. A conversion looks sudden, but the moment that tips it
comes after a long preparation that nobody sees, and the preparation does not
go on in argument.

> When the fruit is ripe, a touch will make it fall.
>
> --- Russ Roberts, after William James

> The change happens below the loquacious level of rationality.
>
> --- Meghan O'Gieblyn, after William James

## Chesterton on Fences and Taboos

**Chesterton's fence.** A reformer finds a fence across a road and wants it
torn down because he sees no use for it. Chesterton's answer is to find out
why it was put there first: a rule whose purpose you cannot see may still be
doing something, and tearing it down can cause a problem somewhere else.

**The unexplained condition.** Roberts reads Chesterton's claim that fairy
tales rest on a taboo nobody explains. Cinderella has to be home by midnight,
and Eve is not to eat the apple. In Chesterton's words as read on the episode,
happiness "depended on not doing something that you could at any moment do and
which very often it was not obvious why you should not do it."

O'Gieblyn connects this to her drinking. The trouble started when she began to
wonder whether the taboo could be negotiated: once the mind tries to reason
about the rule, it can talk itself back into something irrational.

## Change Comes in Circles

> Inner transformation is largely circular in some ways. It's about coming back
> through ritual or successive acts of attention to the same thing and
> reminding yourself of these truths until they sink in.
>
> --- Meghan O'Gieblyn

> Shinto intuits that all life and growth, from galaxies to atomic particles,
> follow the spiral form.
>
> --- On a statue at a Shinto shrine near Seattle
